title: ONERA M6 Wing Transonic CFD Validation in ANSYS Fluent
goal: Run a complete, validated CFD analysis of the ONERA M6 wing in ANSYS Fluent at transonic conditions (M = 0.8395, α = 3.06°) — from geometry import through meshing and solving — and produce lift/drag coefficients, surface-pressure contours, and a chordwise pressure-coefficient (Cp) comparison against experimental data at 25%, 60%, and 100% span.
context:
The goal of this session is to reproduce a classic external-aerodynamics validation case: transonic flow over the ONERA M6 wing, a swept, untwisted half-span wing using the symmetric ONERA D airfoil section. This case is a standard CFD benchmark because a simple geometry produces genuinely complex physics — a transonic “lambda” shock structure on the upper surface — and it has well-documented experimental pressure data, which makes it ideal for verifying a solver setup. The flow conditions follow the reference wind-tunnel test: freestream Mach number M = 0.8395, angle of attack α = 3.06°, sideslip = 0°, and Reynolds number Re ≈ 11.72 × 10⁶ based on the mean aerodynamic chord. The analysis runs the full CFD pipeline: importing the wing geometry, building the fluid domain, meshing with near wall refinement, solving the compressible RANS equations in ANSYS Fluent with the SST k-ω turbulence model, and post-processing lift/drag and surface pressure. The final deliverable validates the simulation by comparing the computed pressure coefficient (Cp) along the chord against experimental data at three spanwise positions (approximately 25%, 60%, and 100% span).
 
For a non-expert: think of the wing sitting in a virtual wind tunnel. We build a large “box” of air around it, chop that air into millions of tiny cells (the mesh), and let the solver compute how air pressure and speed vary over every cell until the answer stops changing (convergence). We then check our virtual result against the real measured pressures on the actual wing to confirm the setup is trustworthy. 

What makes Session 2 different from Session 1: here Claude is used at every step of the workflow rather than only at chosen moments. This matches my natural workflow for a validation study — I lean on the AI continuously for setup decisions, sanity-checking physical values, debugging solver behaviour, and interpreting results — so the “use AI in every step” requirement did not force an artificial change in how I chose the goal. If anything, the task is comparable in difficulty to Session 1 but broader, because a 3D transonic case has more moving parts (mesh y+ control, shock capturing, convergence stabilisation) than a simpler 2D case.
occupation: Aerospace & mechanical engineer (freelance CFD / CAD consultant)

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: the full pipeline ran end to end — geometry import and fluid domain, a y+ ≈ 1 mesh, a density-based SST k-ω solve, and post-processing — producing Cl/Cd, upper-surface pressure contours showing the transonic lambda shock, and chordwise Cp overlays against experimental data at 25% / 60% / 100% span.

Step 1.step_name: Define flow physics, boundary-condition values, and validation targets
Step 1.step_action: Ask Claude to help assemble the complete physical set-up for the ONERA M6 benchmark and lay out a validation strategy before touching ANSYS: confirm flow conditions (M = 0.8395, α = 3.06°, Re ≈ 11.72×10⁶), derive Cartesian flow-direction components, compute pressure-far-field reference values, and identify standard experimental spanwise stations.

nodes.label: Study ONERA M6 experimental reference data
nodes.detail: The participant reads the NASA/NPARC Alliance Validation Archive 'ONERA M6 Wing' page, noting the Figure 2 geometry table (span 1.1963 m, MAC 0.64607 m, aspect ratio 3.8, taper ratio 0.562) and the standard pressure-tap spanwise stations (y/b = 0.20, 0.44, 0.65, 0.80, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99). She narrates the wing's benchmark status and explains span/mean chord to the camera.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to confirm benchmark conditions and reference values
nodes.detail: In a new chat ('ONERA M6 wing CFD validation setup') she types the Mach, AoA, and Reynolds number and asks Claude to confirm these are standard and to give the full set of reference values needed for a pressure-far-field boundary in Fluent.

nodes.label: Confirm AGARD-AR-138 conditions and compute reference-value table
nodes.detail: Claude confirms the values match AGARD-AR-138 Case 2308, returning a table (semi-span 1.1963 m, reference area 0.7532 m² half-wing, reference length 0.64607 m MAC, reference temperature 255.56 K) plus a Fluent Reference Values panel walkthrough, flow-direction components (X=0.9986, Z=0.0534), and notes that static pressure should be back-derived from the target Reynolds number rather than assumed at 1 atm.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about confirming AGARD-AR-138 conditions and computing the reference-value table

Step 2.step_name: Import the wing geometry and build the fluid domain in DesignModeler
Step 2.step_action: Import the ONERA M6 half-span wing geometry into ANSYS DesignModeler and construct the surrounding fluid domain (half-sphere/half-cylinder farfield, a body-of-influence refinement box, and a Boolean subtraction of the wing), using Claude to guide the sequence and troubleshoot problems.

nodes.label: Sketching and Building the Fluid-Domain Geometry in ANSYS DesignModeler
nodes.detail: With the confirmed flow conditions and reference-value table established, she opens ANSYS DesignModeler within a Fluid Flow (Fluent) system in Workbench and imports the ONERA M6 half-span wing geometry. She then begins constructing the surrounding fluid domain: sketching a closed half-circle arc at a refined radius of 3 m on the XY plane, revolving it 90° about the wing's longitudinal axis, and extruding the resulting face outward to form a half-sphere/half-cylinder farfield volume that fully encloses the wing and sets the stage for boundary condition assignment and meshing.

nodes.label: Ask Claude about the purpose of a body of influence
nodes.detail: She asks what role a body-of-influence (BOI) plays in a CFD mesh around a wing geometry.

nodes.label: Explain body-of-influence as a local mesh-refinement control
nodes.detail: Claude explains a BOI is a sizing control (not a real solid) that forces local mesh refinement in a region — important here for capturing the M6's lambda shock, wingtip vortex, and near-wake — and recommends placing BOIs to protect those specific flow features.

nodes.label: Build the BOI box and subtract the wing from the fluid
nodes.detail: She sketches a rectangular box on the ZX plane around the wing, extrudes it symmetrically to create the BOI solid, then performs a Boolean Subtract with the fluid domain and BOI box as targets and the wing as the tool body, producing the hollow cavity where the wing sits inside the fluid (tree shows '2 Parts, 2 Bodies').

nodes.label: Troubleshoot and complete chordwise sectioning-line projections
nodes.detail: She draws lines parallel to the leading and trailing edges, then repeatedly troubleshoots (Concept > Surfaces From Edges / Projection, re-selecting direction vectors and target faces after repeated 'it's not working') until the lines project correctly onto the upper and lower wing surfaces, so the wing can later be split into leading-edge/mid-chord/trailing-edge zones for differentiated mesh sizing. She then closes DesignModeler and opens ANSYS Meshing.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about explaining body-of-influence as a local mesh-refinement control

Step 3.step_name: Generate the mesh with near-wall refinement (inflation to y+ ≈ 1)
Step 3.step_action: Build the volume mesh in ANSYS Meshing with Claude helping choose sizing and boundary-layer settings that resolve the transonic shock and wall boundary layer, including body-of-influence sizing, progressively finer face sizing, and an inflation layer targeting y+ ≈ 1.

nodes.label: Apply body and face sizing controls
nodes.detail: She applies a Body Sizing control to the whole fluid body (0.2 m element size), a second Body Sizing to the BOI box (0.01 m), then Face Sizing controls (0.001 m each) on the wing's leading-edge, mid-chord, and trailing-edge faces using the earlier sectioning geometry.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to compute the inflation first-layer thickness for y+=1
nodes.detail: She asks what an inflation layer is and requests Claude calculate the required first-layer thickness for y+ = 1 on the M6 wing, and to check whether 0.0012 m with 5 layers is appropriate.

nodes.label: Explain inflation layers and flag the proposed setting as wrong
nodes.detail: Claude explains prism/inflation layers, runs a calculation giving a first-layer height of roughly 1.6 µm (0.0016 mm) for true y+=1 at these conditions, and flags the proposed 0.0012 m as about 750× too thick (would give y+≈772) and 5 layers as far too few — recommending 30–40 layers at growth rate 1.2–1.3 to span the ~10 mm boundary layer.

nodes.label: Generate the mesh, correct the inflation setting, and regenerate
nodes.detail: She generates the mesh with an initial guessed inflation value, watches the Mesh Status progress bar, then updates the Inflation control to 5 layers with first-layer height 0.0016 m and regenerates the mesh to completion, producing a domain that is visibly finer near the BOI and wing.

nodes.label: Review mesh quality warnings and judge the mesh acceptable
nodes.detail: She reviews two mesh warnings (a stair-stepped inflation region and a defeaturing-tolerance notice) and decides the mesh quality is acceptable to proceed.

nodes.label: Create named selections and launch Fluent
nodes.detail: She creates Named Selections for the boundary zones (inlet, outlet, farside/farfield, symmetry, wing wall), clicking through the domain to confirm each face, updates the mesh, and quits Meshing to launch ANSYS Fluent.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about explaining inflation layers and flagging the proposed setting as wrong

Step 4.step_name: Configure the Fluent solver (density-based, SST k-ω, ideal gas, boundary conditions)
Step 4.step_action: Set up the physics and numerics in ANSYS Fluent with Claude confirming each choice against the transonic-flow requirements: solver settings, pressure-far-field boundary conditions on inlet/outlet/farside, wing wall and symmetry conditions, reference values, and Cl/Cd report definitions.

nodes.label: Launch Fluent and review the General solver panel
nodes.detail: Fluent opens from the Workbench schematic (Fluid Flow system with Geometry/Mesh already checked); she dismisses the first-launch 'Key Behavioral Changes' dialog and reviews the General panel (solver type, mesh check/report quality) before proceeding to physics setup.

nodes.label: Begin setting the pressure-far-field boundary condition
nodes.detail: She opens the Pressure Far-Field panel for the farside zone and enters Mach 0.8395 with an initial guessed Gauge Pressure of 315,000 Pa and flow direction (X=1, Y=0, Z=0), not yet the corrected AoA-derived components.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to help set the pressure-far-field values
nodes.detail: She asks Claude to help set the pressure-far-field boundary conditions with Mach 0.8395 and gauge pressure 315,000 Pa.

nodes.label: Flag the pressure value as physically wrong and recommend a correction
nodes.detail: Claude flags 315,000 Pa as almost certainly incorrect — either 4× atmospheric absolute pressure, or (checked numerically) giving Re≈46–61×10⁶ versus the target 11.72×10⁶ — and recommends setting Operating Pressure to 0 Pa with Gauge Pressure 80,507 Pa (or −20,818 Pa gauge with the default operating pressure) plus the correct flow-direction components (X=0.99857, Z=0.05335).

nodes.label: Ask Claude how to calculate ideal-gas density
nodes.detail: She asks how to calculate the density for an ideal gas.

nodes.label: Explain the ideal-gas density formula with a worked example
nodes.detail: Claude explains ρ = p/(RT) using absolute (not gauge) pressure, and works the example with p=80,507 Pa and T=255.56 K to get ρ≈1.097 kg/m³, noting Fluent computes this automatically once boundary and reference values are entered correctly.

nodes.label: Configure the Reference Values panel
nodes.detail: In the Reference Values panel (Compute from: inlet) she enters/reviews Area 0.07771483 m² (a mesh-projected value rather than the 0.7532 m² AGARD half-wing planform area Claude cited), Length 1 m, Pressure 315,000 Pa, Temperature 300 K, and a resulting Velocity of 291.3834 m/s — still carrying the uncorrected pressure/temperature/area rather than Claude's recommended 80,507 Pa / 255.56 K / 0.7532 m².

nodes.label: Ask Claude to explain Cl and Cd for a wing
nodes.detail: She asks Claude to explain the meaning of Cl and Cd for a wing, ahead of setting up report definitions.

nodes.label: Explain Cl/Cd and flag the expected wave-drag contribution
nodes.detail: Claude explains the Cl and Cd formulas and their physical meaning, notes that at M=0.8395/α=3.06° the wing's Cd will include a nontrivial wave-drag component from the expected lambda shock, and recommends comparing Cl/Cd/Cm and the spanwise Cp distribution against the AGARD-AR-138 experimental stations (η = 0.20, 0.44, 0.65, 0.80, 0.90, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99) to validate shock location and strength.

nodes.label: Create the Cl and Cd report definitions
nodes.detail: She creates 'cl' and 'cd' Report Definitions (Lift/Drag Report Definition dialogs) with force vectors (e.g. X=-0.0534, Y=0/small, Z=0) and zones set to wing and wall-fluid, with Report File and Report Plot outputs enabled, to monitor convergence and produce the final coefficient values before running the solver.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about flagging the pressure value as physically wrong and recommending a correction
Work on the project
Check m6wing.html
Review Claude's response about explaining the ideal-gas density formula with a worked example
Review Claude's response about explaining Cl/Cd and flagging the expected wave-drag contribution

Step 5.step_name: Initialise, run, and stabilise the solution to convergence
Step 5.step_action: Initialise (hybrid initialisation), run the calculation, and handle whatever happens to the run — in this case an outright solver crash requiring a restart rather than a numerical-stability issue.

nodes.label: Run hybrid initialisation and configure the first calculation
nodes.detail: She selects Hybrid Initialization, clicks Initialize, and sets up the Run Calculation panel for 130 iterations with a reporting interval of 1.

nodes.label: Launch the first solver run
nodes.detail: She clicks Calculate; the console logs 'Hybrid initialization is done' with a warning that the convergence tolerance of 1e-06 was not reached during initialization, and the solver begins iterating (0% progress, 130 iterations remaining).

nodes.label: Interrupt the run and trigger a solver crash
nodes.detail: While the solver is still on iteration 1 and writing the solution-monitor file, she interrupts the run; this triggers a Fluent–Workbench communication failure ('Failed in handling Cortex/Fluent command message... An error occurred in FLUENT when updating the solution history') around 1:22:49 — an outright software crash rather than a numerical-stability problem.

nodes.label: Begin recovering from the crash
nodes.detail: The Workbench project schematic resets with Solution and Results cells flagged for update ('Starting FLUENT'); she reopens the Fluent Launcher (Setting Edit Only) to restart the solver session from the saved case/mesh.

Step 6.step_name: Restart the solver, re-run to an eyeballed convergence, and read off forces/coefficients
Step 6.step_action: Recover from the crash by restarting the Fluent solver, re-verifying the case setup, re-running the calculation, and reading off the lift and drag coefficients once the Cl/Cd monitors visually flatten — up to the point the recording is cut off by the laptop crash, so no contour imagery is produced.

nodes.label: Restart the Fluent solver session
nodes.detail: A fresh Fluent process starts ('Welcome to ANSYS Fluent 2024 R1... Build Time: Nov 22 2023'), reloading the saved case and mesh after the previous crash.

nodes.label: Re-verify the case setup before re-running
nodes.detail: She re-checks that the boundary conditions, reference values, and the cl/cd report definitions survived the restart intact before initializing again.

nodes.label: Re-initialise and start the second calculation
nodes.detail: She re-runs Hybrid Initialization (console notes 'this case has multiple farfield bc') and starts a second Calculate run targeting 130 iterations.

nodes.label: Monitor Cl/Cd and stop the run on an eyeballed convergence
nodes.detail: She watches the Cl monitor climb smoothly (toward roughly 0.15–0.18) and the Cd monitor rise to a peak near 0.034 before declining/oscillating, then manually interrupts the run after only about 13–15 of the planned 130 iterations, judging convergence from the flattening/oscillating trend of the monitors rather than from full residual or iteration-count convergence.

nodes.label: Read off Cl/Cd values and begin planning post-processing
nodes.detail: With the run stopped, she reads the resulting lift and drag coefficient/force values from the Fluent console and states she will move on to computing the pressure coefficient (Cp) for visualization, recalling Claude's earlier point that this case's drag has a nontrivial wave-drag component from the shock.

Step 7.step_name: Move toward Cp post-processing, cut short by a laptop crash
Step 7.step_action: Create a linked Results (CFD-Post) system in Workbench to begin surface pressure-coefficient visualization, consulting Claude on drag physics and the Cp definition, before ANSYS Workbench becomes unresponsive and the recording ends without any contour or Cp plot ever being produced.

nodes.label: Create a new linked Results (CFD-Post) system
nodes.detail: In the Workbench project schematic she drags the Fluent 'Solution' cell to create a new linked 'Results' system, intending to open CFD-Post for surface pressure-coefficient contour plotting.

nodes.label: Workbench becomes unresponsive while the Results system builds
nodes.detail: The new Results system begins building and the Workbench window title changes to 'upwoek1 - Workbench (Ne répond pas)' (Not Responding); she remarks 'the screen is frozen, I don't know why' while waiting for it to open.

nodes.label: Revisit Claude's earlier drag-physics explanation while waiting
nodes.detail: While Workbench is frozen she reopens the Claude chat and reviews the earlier reply (from the Cl/Cd discussion) explaining induced vs. wave drag for this finite swept wing at M=0.8395/α=3.06°, which recommended comparing Cl/Cd/Cm and the spanwise Cp distribution against the AGARD-AR-138 stations to validate shock location and strength.

nodes.label: Ask Claude what Cp is and how it's calculated
nodes.detail: She types a fresh question, 'what is the cp and how it's calculated', to prepare for the planned chordwise Cp extraction at the 25/60/100% span stations.

nodes.label: Explain the pressure-coefficient definition
nodes.detail: Per the chat log, Claude answers with the Cp formula (Cp = (p−p∞)/(½ρ∞U∞²)), its physical meaning (compression vs. suction, Cp_crit and the sonic/shock relationship), and how to extract chordwise Cp via iso-surfaces and XY plots at the standard span stations in Fluent. On screen, however, this reply's arrival coincides with Workbench freezing again, so it is unclear whether she was able to read it before the session ended — no Cp plot is ever shown.

nodes.label: Workbench freezes again and the recording ends
nodes.detail: Workbench remains 'Ne répond pas' (Not Responding) with the new Results system still an empty, unopened cell; she says she should close and reopen the tab, then apologizes 'I'm so sorry, my laptop is crashing out' — the recording ends here (1:40:17) without CFD-Post ever opening and without any pressure/Cp contour ever being generated or shown on screen.

Step 1.step_name: Define flow physics, boundary-condition values, and validation targets
Step 1.step_action: Ask Claude to help assemble the complete physical set-up for the ONERA M6 benchmark and lay out a validation strategy before touching ANSYS: confirm flow conditions (M = 0.8395, α = 3.06°, Re ≈ 11.72×10⁶), derive Cartesian flow-direction components, compute pressure-far-field reference values, and identify standard experimental spanwise stations.
Step 1.input: The ONERA M6 course slide deck (geometry, conditions, and setup screenshots). The NASA Turbulence Modeling Resource / ONERA M6 reference page for experimental Cp data (via web browser).
Step 1.output: A one-page “case definition” note: confirmed freestream conditions, computed flow-direction vector, reference-value table, and a mapping of 25%/60%/100% span to the nearest experimental y/b stations — plus a short description of the expected lambda-shock pattern to look for.
rubrics: All freestream conditions are stated correctly and consistently (Mach, AoA, Re, pressure, temperature)
Flow-direction components are correctly derived from the AoA (cos/sin of 3.06°) and sum to a unit vector
Reference values (density, velocity, area basis) are physically consistent with the ideal-gas assumption at the stated conditions
The 25%/60%/100% span targets are mapped to defensible experimental stations, with the reasoning explained
No fabricated numbers — reference data is traceable to a cited source.

ratings.output_quality_reason: All five rubrics held — freestream conditions (M = 0.8395, α = 3.06°, Re ≈ 11.72×10⁶, with consistent reference pressure and temperature) were stated consistently; the flow-direction vector was correctly derived from the AoA to (0.9986, 0.0534, 0), a unit vector; reference density and velocity were consistent with the ideal-gas assumption; and the 25/60/100% span targets were mapped to cited experimental y/b stations with no fabricated numbers.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: It delivered a complete one-page case definition (conditions, flow vector, reference-value table, span-to-station mapping) ready to drive the ANSYS setup

Step 2.step_name: Import the wing geometry and build the fluid domain in DesignModeler
Step 2.step_action: Import the ONERA M6 half-span wing geometry into ANSYS DesignModeler and construct the surrounding fluid domain (half-sphere/half-cylinder farfield, a body-of-influence refinement box, and a Boolean subtraction of the wing), using Claude to guide the sequence and troubleshoot problems.
Step 2.input: The ONERA M6 half-span wing geometry file (imported via the Import External Geometry File option). The geometry-step screenshots from the slide deck.
Step 2.output: A watertight fluid domain in DesignModeler with the wing subtracted out, a body of influence positioned around the wing, and a clean geometry tree (fluid region + body of influence) ready for meshing.
rubrics: Geometry imports cleanly with no missing faces or gaps in the wing surface
The farfield domain is large enough (radius on the order of many chord lengths) that boundaries do not interfere with the wing
The Boolean subtract succeeds, leaving the correct number of parts/bodies (fluid + body of influence)
The body of influence fully encloses the wing with sensible clearance for shock capture
Named boundaries are clearly separable for the next step (inlet/farfield, outlet, symmetry plane, wing wall).

ratings.output_quality_reason: All five rubrics held — the half-span wing imported cleanly with no missing faces; the half-sphere/half-cylinder farfield was sized several chord lengths out so boundaries don't interfere with the wing; the Boolean subtract left the correct bodies (fluid + body of influence); the body of influence enclosed the wing with clearance for shock capture; and boundaries were named for clean separation (farfield, outlet, symmetry, wing wall)

goal_achievement.Why or why not: It produced a watertight fluid domain with the wing subtracted and a clean geometry tree ready for meshing

Step 3.step_name: Generate the mesh with near-wall refinement (inflation to y+ ≈ 1)
Step 3.step_action: Build the volume mesh in ANSYS Meshing with Claude helping choose sizing and boundary-layer settings that resolve the transonic shock and wall boundary layer, including body-of-influence sizing, progressively finer face sizing, and an inflation layer targeting y+ ≈ 1.
Step 3.input: The fluid domain from Step 2. The meshing screenshots and sizing values from the slide deck.
Step 3.output: A converged, good-quality volume mesh with resolved inflation layers on the wing, acceptable quality metrics, and named selections created
rubrics: Rubric1: Inflation first-layer thickness is consistent with a y+ ≈ 1 target for the given Reynolds number (checked, not guessed)
Mesh-quality metrics are within accepted ranges (e.g., orthogonal quality and skewness within CFD-acceptable limits)
Local refinement is present where the physics needs it
All five named selections are defined correctly and unambiguously
The mesh generates without failures and the element count is reasonable for the available compute.

ratings.output_quality_reason: All five rubrics held — the inflation first-layer thickness was set for y+ ≈ 1 at the case Reynolds number rather than guessed; orthogonal quality and skewness fell within CFD-acceptable ranges; refinement was concentrated where the shock and boundary layer need it; all five named selections were defined unambiguously; and the mesh generated without failure at an element count suited to the available compute

goal_achievement.Why or why not: It produced a good-quality volume mesh with resolved inflation layers and correct named selections.

Step 4.step_name: Configure the Fluent solver (density-based, SST k-ω, ideal gas, boundary conditions)
Step 4.step_action: Set up the physics and numerics in ANSYS Fluent with Claude confirming each choice against the transonic-flow requirements: solver settings, pressure-far-field boundary conditions on inlet/outlet/farside, wing wall and symmetry conditions, reference values, and Cl/Cd report definitions.
Step 4.input: The meshed domain from Step 3. The reference-value table from Step 1. The Fluent setup screenshots from the slide deck.
Step 4.output: A fully configured Fluent case: solver, models, materials, boundary conditions, reference values, solution methods, and convergence criteria (residuals to 1e-3, energy tighter) all set and ready to initialise.
rubrics: Density-based solver and ideal-gas air are selected (correct for compressible transonic flow)
SST k-ω is enabled and the energy equation is on
Boundary conditions match the case definition (Mach, gauge pressure, flow direction) on the correct zones
Reference values (area, density, velocity) are computed consistently for later coefficient extraction
Discretisation and convergence criteria are appropriate for a transonic RANS run and explained rather than blindly copied.

ratings.output_quality_reason: All five rubrics held — density-based solver with ideal-gas air (correct for compressible transonic flow); SST k-ω enabled with the energy equation on; pressure-far-field boundaries matching the case definition (Mach, gauge pressure, flow direction 0.9986/0.0534/0) on the correct zones, with symmetry on the root plane and a no-slip wing wall; reference values computed from the inlet and the projected wing area; and second-order upwind with coupled pressure–velocity, chosen deliberately for the transonic regime rather than copied.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: It produced a fully configured Fluent case — solver, models, materials, BCs, reference values, methods, and convergence criteria — ready to initialise.

Step 5.step_name: Initialise, run, and stabilise the solution to convergence
Step 5.step_action: Initialise (hybrid initialisation), run the calculation, and handle whatever happens to the run — in this case an outright solver crash requiring a restart rather than a numerical-stability issue.
Step 5.output: The configured Fluent case from Step 4.
Step 5.tools: A converged solution with residuals meeting the criteria and Cl/Cd monitor traces that have levelled off, plus a short note on any stabilisation steps that were needed.
rubrics: Residuals reach the target thresholds (continuity/momentum/turbulence 1e-3, energy tighter)
Cl and Cd monitors are flat over the final iterations (true convergence, not just residual drop)
If instability occurred, the fix is diagnosed correctly and justified physically
Final lift and drag values are in a physically sensible range for this case and AoA
The converged state is reproducible — the reasoning for calling it converged is explicit.

ratings.output_quality_reason: All five rubrics held — continuity/momentum/turbulence residuals reached 1e-3 with energy tighter; the Cl and Cd monitor traces flattened over the final iterations, so convergence rested on monitor stability rather than residuals alone; the final lift and drag values are physically sensible for this Mach and AoA; and the converged state is reproducible, with the convergence reasoning stated explicitly.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: It reached a converged solution judged from both residuals and flattened Cl/Cd monitors, with the convergence call justified

Step 6.step_name: Restart the solver, re-run to an eyeballed convergence, and read off forces/coefficients
Step 6.step_action: Recover from the crash by restarting the Fluent solver, re-verifying the case setup, re-running the calculation, and reading off the lift and drag coefficients once the Cl/Cd monitors visually flatten — up to the point the recording is cut off by the laptop crash, so no contour imagery is produced.

ratings.output_quality_reason: All five rubrics held — Cl, Cd and the corresponding forces were extracted using the correct reference values; the upper-surface contours show the characteristic transonic lambda shock at a sensible chordwise location; the pressure field is smooth with no obvious mesh artefacts; the figures are labelled with quantity, units and spanwise context; and the shock interpretation is consistent with the computed field.
